Abstract.text: Alzheimer’s disease is the leading cause of dementia, and early detection of its biomarkers, such as amyloid-beta (Aβ) and tau protein, may be key to delaying its onset. We aim to develop an aptamer-based electrochemical biosensor for the detection of amyloid-beta 42 (Aβ42). Our sensor uses a methylene blue-labelled DNA aptamer that undergoes a conformational change when it binds Aβ42, producing a signal measured by differential pulse voltammetry (DPV). Previous work has identified dendrimers as signal amplifiers for electrochemical biosensors; building on this, we identified a polyamidoamine (PAMAM) dendrimer as a structural backbone that could also reduce noise in our DPV signal. We also implemented toehold-mediated strand displacement (TMSD) so that the aptamer can be exchanged. We demonstrated the efficacy of our biosensor by identifying unknown samples using a calibration curve, which showed that the sensor is accurate in an analytical solution. We then confirmed this accuracy in a blood-mimetic solution, showing that the sensor is applicable in a point-of-care setting. By enabling early detection, this biosensor could allow Alzheimer’s screening to be scaled up to population-wide testing and help delay onset by informing risk-targeted interventions for improving brain fitness.
